modern_lens_framing: The Qurʾan is taken here as fixed, revealed truth; science is our provisional, evolving account of the observable world. What follows notes where the two meet — a contemplation, not a proof. Where the science later shifts, that reflects the limits of our knowledge, not the text.

102:5.title: Seeing Hell With Certain Eyes
102:5.in_short: The surah warns that if people truly grasped the coming reckoning with certainty, mere rivalry in wealth would never have distracted them. They will surely see Hellfire, and then see it again with the certainty that only direct sight gives.

claims.text: "Kallā" (No indeed!) is a strong rebuke and check, repeated through the surah, each time followed by a further warning, as if saying: do not do this, for you will regret it.

102:5.essay_html:
"No indeed!" says the verse, a sharp check on what has just been said about rivalry in wealth. The commentators read this as a rebuke, repeated through the surah, each occurrence followed by a further warning, as though saying: do not carry on like this, for you will regret it.1,3

The sentence "if only you knew for certain" leaves its main clause unstated. The sense understood by the commentators is plain: if people truly knew with certainty, they would never have been distracted by competing over wealth, and would instead have hastened to good deeds.1,2,3,7,9,11,12,14 Qatāda explained this certain knowledge as knowing for sure that Allah will raise everyone up after death.1,2 Other reports attribute to him that "certainty" here means death itself, or else the resurrection, since once it arrives all doubt disappears.3 Grammatically, the phrase joins "knowledge" to "certainty", much as the Qur'an elsewhere speaks of "the truth of certainty".2,3,9

Some commentators set out three rising degrees of certainty behind this word. "'Ilm al-yaqīn" is certainty gained through knowledge or reasoning, as when one sees smoke from afar and infers a fire. "'Ayn al-yaqīn" is certainty gained by actually seeing the thing with one's own eyes. "Ḥaqq al-yaqīn" is certainty gained through direct contact, as when one touches the fire or enters it.8,9 Sayyid Qutb (d. 1966) notes that the repetition of such frightening words, each followed by something weightier, deepens the warning, though the heedless miss its force because they are lost in intoxication, busy day and night gathering wealth.6 Behind this stands a wider theme drawn from hadith: love of the world distracts a person until death, yet the true benefit of wealth is only what is eaten, worn, or given away, everything else passes on while the reckoning for it only grows.4,10 Had people truly known this, they would have restrained themselves and hurried to save themselves from ruin.13

"You will most definitely see Hellfire" is read two ways by the reciters. Most read it as "you will surely see", while al-Kisā'ī and Ibn 'Āmir read it as "you will surely be shown"; al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) held the majority reading correct on grounds of scholarly agreement.1,2,3 The statement answers an implied oath: "by Allah, you will surely see the Fire" in the Hereafter.3,9,12 The address is understood by some to fall on the disbelievers specifically, those for whom the Fire is due, and Ibn 'Abbās (d. 687) is reported to have said this verse concerns the people of shirk.1,3 Others hold the address is general, since "there is not one of you who will not come to it", recalling a hadith describing people crossing over Hell, some like lightning, some like wind, some like birds.3 At this stage the seeing is still with the eyes from a distance.2,3

Then comes the second sighting: "you will see it with the eye of certainty." This phrase means direct, unmistakable eyewitness observation, the highest degree of certainty, since it comes from actually seeing rather than from report or inference.2,3,5,7,9,12 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) and Abū Bakr Zakariyyā relate a report from Ibn 'Abbās that news is never like eyewitnessing: when Mūsā عليه السلام was on the mountain and told that his people had taken to worshipping the calf, it did not shake him as it did when he returned and saw it himself, so much that the Tablets fell from his hands and broke.7,11 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) records further readings: that this describes the permanence of the disbelievers' presence in the Fire, an unbroken seeing rather than a glimpse, or that certain knowledge in this world lets a person see Hellfire already with the eye of the heart, before the physical eye confirms it beyond doubt in the Hereafter.3 One source adds that the first sighting was from a distance, while this second sighting comes from close up.12 After this comes, in what follows, a question about every blessing enjoyed.13

What is presented first as a claim to be reasoned about becomes, in the end, a thing to be seen with one's own eyes, and the commentators read the surah's rising language, knowledge, then a first sight, then a certain sight, as tracing exactly that movement from hearing to witnessing.1,2,3,5,7,8,9

102:1.title: The Race for More
102:1.in_short: The surah warns that the human race for 'more' — wealth, children, numbers, status — blinds people until death itself catches them, and it tells them twice over that they will come to know the truth of what occupied them.

102:1.essay_html:
The surah opens on a single human failing: chasing 'more' (al-Takāthur, rivalry in increase) diverts people from what actually matters. The word for 'distracts' comes from lahw, meaning to be made heedless.1,3,9,11,12 One commentator notes that the object of the rivalry is left unnamed on purpose, so the verse can cover whatever people compete over: wealth, children, supporters, armies, servants, status.5,11 The exegetes record different readings of exactly what is meant: Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan take it as wealth and children, Qatadah as pride in tribe and clan numbers, al-Dahhak as preoccupation with livelihood and trade.1,3,7

Several reports describe the occasion behind the verse. One says it concerned a group who kept boasting 'we outnumber such-and-such tribe' while dying off one by one, until they had all become people of the graves themselves.1,2,3 Another names two clans of Quraysh, Banu Abd Manaf and Banu Sahm, who competed first over their living nobles, then went out to the graves and counted their dead by name, Banu Sahm winning by three graves.2,3 Other reports point to a branch of the Ansar, to merchants, or to the People of the Book. Al-Qurţubī (d. 1273) says the verse is broad enough to hold all of these readings and more.3

A group of reports carry the Prophet's ţ's own explanation. He is reported to have recited the verse and said that the son of Adam claims 'my wealth, my wealth', yet truly owns nothing of it except what he ate and finished, wore and wore out, or gave away and sent ahead of himself; everything else passes to other people.1,2,3,4,7,9,11 Ubayy b. Ka'b said the companions once thought a related saying, that a person given a valley of gold would still want a second and that nothing but grave-dust fills his mouth, was itself part of the Qur'an, until this surah was revealed with the same meaning.1,3,4,7 Another hadith says three things follow the dead, his family, his wealth, and his deeds; the first two turn back, and only his deeds remain with him.2,4 One report even has the Prophet ţ saying he feared abundance for his people more than he feared poverty.11 A further report gives this short surah the weight of a thousand verses.7

Behind all this, al-Sa'dī (d. 1957) reads the distraction as being from the very purpose of creation: worship of God alone, knowledge of Him, and turning to Him in love above everything else.5 Later commentators put it in plainer terms: the appetite for more is never satisfied, and the chase does not stop until death itself intervenes.6,8,10 One draws a line to Surah al-Ḥadīd 57:20, where the last stage of human life described there is precisely this competition in wealth and children, a greed that grows rather than fades with age.8

The verse says 'until you visited the graves', not 'until you settled there'. Several commentators draw out that a visitor eventually leaves, so the grave is read as a temporary stop, not the final residence.3,5,9,11 Al-Qurţubī adds that the word for graves appears in the Qur'an only in this surah, and goes on to discuss hadiths that recommend visiting graves as a reminder of death.3 Some take the verse further, as a pointer to the punishment of the grave: Ali (رضي الله عنه) is reported to have said, 'we used to doubt the punishment of the grave, until this surah was revealed.'1,3

'Kalla' (No indeed) then interrupts, a rebuke: this rivalry is not how one ought to have lived.1,3,9,13 The warning that follows, 'you will come to know', is said twice. The commentators explain the repetition as the ordinary Arabic way of sharpening a threat, warning laid upon warning.1,3,9,12,14 They differ over what the two moments of knowing point to. Ibn Abbas took the first as the punishment of the grave and the second as that of the Hereafter, while Mujahid read it simply as one threat doubled rather than two separate events.3 Al-Dahhak had his own distinctive reading, taking the first warning as addressed to the disbelievers and the second to the believers, and reciting the two verbs with different grammatical forms to match.1,2,3 Al-Muyassar paraphrases the pair as: you will come to see that the Hereafter is better than what distracted you, so beware the outcome of that neglect.13

Across these readings the same picture returns: a life spent competing over 'more', that ends, as the Prophet ţ is reported to have said, with a person owning nothing of his wealth beyond what he ate, wore, or gave away.1,2,3,4,7,9,11

102:8.title: Questioned About Every Pleasure
102:8.in_short: The sūra ends with the announcement that on the Day of Judgment every person will be questioned about the pleasures and favours (al-Naʿīm) enjoyed in this life, how they were earned, used, and whether thanks was given for them.

claims.text: The verse means that on the Day of Judgment God will question people about the favours and pleasures they had in this world: how they obtained them, what they did with them, and whether they gave thanks for them.

original_terms.gloss: the pleasures / favours a person enjoyed in worldly life

claims.text: Early commentators differed over exactly what 'the pleasures' refers to. Some said it means security and bodily health.
Others said it means the faculties of hearing, sight and the soundness of the body which God granted, linking it to the verse that the ear, the eye and the heart will each be questioned.
Others said it is well-being (al-ʿāfiya), or health together with free time (al-farāgh), or health, free time and wealth together.
Others took it as food and drink specifically enjoyed, illustrated by reports of the Prophet ﷺ pointing to particular meals as instances of the naʿīm that will be questioned.
Others said it covers everything a person delighted in during worldly life without restriction — food, clothing, house, spouse, children, rule, or honour, as Mujāhid held.
Still others read it as Islam and the Sunna, the lightening of the Sharia and the ease of the Qurʾān, or specifically the favour of Muḥammad ﷺ having been sent as a messenger.
A hadith cited by al-Qurṭubī also counts one's worldly standing or rank (jāh) among what will be asked about, since God questions a servant about his rank just as He questions him about his wealth.

Al-Ṭabarī, after listing these views, states the soundest reading is that the wording is unrestricted: God said He would question them about the naʿīm without limiting it to one kind, so the questioning covers every sort of favour, not some at the expense of others. Al-Qurṭubī likewise calls the comprehensive reading the best, since the wording is general, and Muftī Shafīʿ cites both in agreement.

Some held that this questioning is directed only at disbelievers, since al-Ḥasan said only the people of the Fire are asked about the naʿīm, and a report has Abū Bakr رضي الله عنه worry about a meal he shared with the Prophet ﷺ, to which the Prophet ﷺ replied that this reckoning belongs to the disbelievers, then recited the verse about the disbelievers never being repaid except with their disbelief.

report.graded_by: reported via al-Qushayrī, cited by al-Qurṭubī without a formal grading

claims.text: Others reconciled the reports: everyone, believer and disbeliever, will be asked, but the disbeliever's questioning is a rebuke for having failed to give thanks, while the believer's questioning is an honouring, since he did give thanks. This reconciliation, attributed to al-Qushayrī and approved by al-Qurṭubī, is also cited approvingly by al-Ṭanṭāwī, and the same two positions (only disbelievers vs. everyone) are set out by Ahsanul Bayaan, which notes that being questioned does not by itself mean punishment: a person who used the favours as God commanded will be kept safe from punishment despite being asked.

A minority view held that this specific questioning was directed at the disbelievers of Mecca, who lived in worldly wealth and comfort but did not thank the Giver of that favour, since they worshipped others besides Him, and will be punished for withholding that gratitude. This was said to be al-Ḥasan's position as reported through Muqātil.

Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda held that three basic necessities are excluded from this questioning: a garment to cover one's nakedness, a piece of bread that staves off hunger, and shelter that gives cover. A hadith likewise lists these as exceptions to what a servant will be asked about.

report.graded_by: narrated through multiple chains in al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī without an explicit grading

claims.text: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna argued that whatever merely staves off hunger and covers nakedness in coarse food and clothing is not questioned, drawing on the fact that God settled Adam عليه السلام in Paradise promising he would not hunger, go naked, thirst, or suffer heat there — meaning these four basic needs were unconditionally granted to Adam and are therefore not reckoned.

A widely reported narrative recounts the Prophet ﷺ, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar رضي الله عنهما leaving their houses out of hunger and being fed dates, meat, and cool water at the home of a companion (named as Abū al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihān, whose given name was Mālik). The Prophet ﷺ told them afterward that this very meal, its cool shade, ripe dates, and cool water, was itself among the naʿīm they would be asked about on the Day of Judgment.

report.graded_by: recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, per al-Qurṭubī's citation

claims.text: Another report says that when this verse was revealed, some of the Companions (or 'the people') asked the Prophet ﷺ which naʿīm they would be questioned about, since they had only dates and water, swords on their shoulders, and the enemy before them. The Prophet ﷺ replied that this questioning would indeed come to pass.

report.graded_by: cited via al-Tirmidhī by al-Qurṭubī and others without a stated grading

claims.text: A hadith states that the first thing a servant will be asked about among the favours on Judgment Day is: 'Did We not restore your body to health, and did We not give you cool water to drink?'

report.graded_by: al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Ḥibbān, as cited by Ibn Kathīr and relayed by Muftī Shafīʿ

claims.text: A further hadith, reported from Bukhari, states that no person will be able to move from his place on Judgment Day until he answers five things: how he spent his life, how he spent his youth, how he earned his wealth, how he spent it, and whether he acted on the knowledge God gave him.

report.graded_by: al-Bukhārī, as cited by Muftī Shafīʿ

claims.text: Al-Saʿdī and al-Ṭanṭāwī explain that the substance of the questioning is whether a person gave thanks for the favour, fulfilled God's right in it, and refrained from using it to disobey Him, in which case he is given a still higher favour, or whether he was deceived by it, failed to give thanks, and perhaps even used it to disobey God, in which case he is punished, as in the verse describing disbelievers shown the Fire and told: 'you enjoyed your good things in worldly life, so today you are repaid with a degrading punishment.'

Sayyid Quṭb describes the questioning in fuller detail: where the wealth or favour came from, how it was spent, whether it was earned and used in obedience or disobedience to God, through lawful or unlawful means, whether its due of gratitude was fulfilled, whether it was shared with others or hoarded selfishly, and how it was gathered and boasted over. He stresses that these pleasures look light and trivial to the heedless, yet carry behind them a heavy responsibility and a harsh reckoning.

Ibn Kathīr connects the sūra's closing warning to a set of related hadiths on the nature of wealth: a servant truly benefits from only three things out of his wealth, what he ate and consumed, what he wore until worn out, and what he gave in charity; everything else passes on to others after him. Likewise, three things follow the deceased to the grave, his family, his wealth and his deeds, but only his deeds remain with him. And even as a person grows old, two things stay with him: greed and hope for more.

Wahīduddīn Khān observes that man remains absorbed in accumulating more and more, mistaking this increase for success, until death. Only after death does he realise that what deserved to be treasured was something else, but by then the realisation comes too late to be of any use.

102:8.essay_html:
The sūra closes with a single reckoning: every person will be questioned about the pleasures they enjoyed in this world, how those pleasures were earned, how they were spent, and whether thanks was given for them.1,5,6,7,8,9,11,12,13,14

Commentators differed on exactly what 'the pleasures' (al-Naʿīm) means. Some said security and bodily health.1,2,3 Others pointed to hearing, sight and the soundness of the body, tying it to the verse that the ear, the eye and the heart will each be questioned.1,2,3,7,11 Others named well-being, or health together with free time, or health, free time and wealth combined.1,2,3 Some read it as the food and drink one enjoyed, others as Islam, the Sunna, the ease of the Sharīʿa, or the very favour of Muḥammad ﷺ being sent.1,2,3 One report even counts a person's worldly rank (jāh) among what is asked about.3 Mujāhid took it further still: every worldly delight without exception, food, clothing, house, spouse, children, rule, honour.1,3,7

Al-Ṭabarī, after setting out these views, judged that the soundest reading is the widest one: the wording is unrestricted, so the questioning covers every kind of favour, not one type at the expense of another. Al-Qurṭubī reaches the same conclusion, and Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ relays both in agreement.1,3,7

A separate question occupied the commentators: is this reckoning for disbelievers alone, or for everyone? Al-Ḥasan held that only the people of the Fire are asked about the naʿīm, and a report has Abū Bakr رضي الله عنه worried about a shared meal, to which the Prophet ﷺ answered that this reckoning belongs to the disbelievers.3,12 Others reconciled the two positions: everyone is asked, but for the disbeliever it is a rebuke, since he withheld thanks, while for the believer it is an honouring, since he gave thanks. Al-Qurṭubī favours this reconciliation, al-Ṭanṭāwī repeats it approvingly, and the point that being questioned does not itself mean punishment is echoed elsewhere.3,9,12 Al-Baghawī records a further reading, that the verse addresses the disbelievers of Mecca specifically, who had worldly comfort but did not thank its true Giver.2

Some necessities were said to fall outside this reckoning altogether. Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda named three: a garment for covering nakedness, a piece of bread that staves off hunger, and shelter. A hadith lists the same exceptions.1,3 Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna grounded the exemption in the story of Adam عليه السلام, who was promised in Paradise that he would not hunger, thirst, go naked, or suffer heat, these four needs being freely given rather than reckoned.3

A well-known narrative brings the point home. The Prophet ﷺ, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar رضي الله عنهما left their houses out of hunger and were fed dates, meat and cool water at a companion's home. The Prophet ﷺ told them afterward that this very meal, its shade, its ripe dates, its cool water, was itself part of the naʿīm they would be asked about.1,2,3,11,14 Another report has the Companions protest, when the verse was revealed, that they possessed only dates and water, with swords on their shoulders and the enemy before them, asking which naʿīm could this concern. The Prophet ﷺ answered that the questioning would indeed come to pass.1,3,11,14 A further hadith names the very first question put to a servant: 'Did We not restore your body to health, and give you cool water to drink?'1,2,3,7,11,14 and Muftī Shafīʿ relays from Bukhārī that no one moves from his place until he answers how he spent his life, his youth, his wealth and its earning, and what he did with knowledge.7

Al-Saʿdī and al-Ṭanṭāwī describe the substance of the questioning: did the person thank God for the favour and fulfil His right in it, or was he deceived by it, ungrateful, perhaps even using it to disobey, a path that ends as in the verse describing disbelievers told 'you enjoyed your good things in worldly life, so today you are repaid with a degrading punishment.'5,9 Sayyid Quṭb widens this into a full audit: where the wealth came from, how it was spent, lawful or unlawful, obedient or defiant, shared or hoarded, gathered honestly or boasted over, favours that look light and trivial to the heedless but carry, he says, a heavy responsibility and a harsh reckoning.6

Ibn Kathīr closes the theme with related hadiths on wealth itself: a person truly keeps only three things from his wealth, what he ate, what he wore out, and what he gave in charity, everything else passing to others; three things follow the dead to the grave, family, wealth and deeds, but only deeds remain with him; and even in old age, greed and hope for more stay behind when everything else fades.4 Wahīduddīn Khān adds that man spends his life chasing accumulation, mistaking it for success, and only realises after death what was truly worth keeping, a realisation that by then can do him no good.10

The sūra that opened with the distraction of counting more ends with a single account to be settled: every pleasure, however small, will be named and asked about.
